title: Test gear: multimeter, clamp meter, oscilloscope
goals: Connect a meter the right way for volts, amps and ohms, and say why amps across a supply is dangerous
Choose a meter and leads with the right CAT rating, and prove a circuit dead
Read a current with a clamp meter, and say why round a whole cable it reads nearly zero
Read a waveform's frequency and peak-to-peak voltage from an oscilloscope's divisions
Say why a mains scope's earth clip must not go on a live point
summary:
**Volts**: across the part, in parallel. **Amps**: in series, the circuit broken to put the meter in it; on an amps range the meter is nearly a short circuit, so amps across a supply blows the meter's fuse (or worse). **Ohms**: only on a dead circuit.

**CAT ratings** (IEC 61010) say where a meter can safely go: **CAT II** at sockets and plug-in appliances, **CAT III** in the fixed installation (distribution boards, hard-wired motors, panels), **CAT IV** at the origin (the supply intake, meters, overhead lines). Use one rated for the highest place you could use it, at or above the voltage.

**HSE GS38** leads: shrouded probes with finger guards, no more than 4 mm of exposed tip (2 mm or less preferred), fused or current-limited.

**Prove dead** with an approved two-pole voltage indicator: prove it on a known live source, test the circuit (every conductor to every other and to earth), prove it again.

A **clamp meter** reads current from the magnetic field round **one** conductor. Round L and N together (or all three phases), the fields cancel and it reads nearly zero: only leakage.

**True RMS** meters read distorted currents (drives, switch-mode supplies) correctly; average-responding meters can be well out.

An **oscilloscope** draws voltage (up, in volts per division) against time (across, in time per division). Period = divisions × time per division; frequency = 1 ÷ period. Peak-to-peak = divisions × volts per division.

A mains-powered scope's probe **earth clip is connected to earth**. Clip it to a point that is not at earth and you make a short circuit through the probe. Use a differential probe or an isolated-channel scope for anything not earth-referenced.

formulas.name: Period from the scope's divisions
formulas.says: Count the divisions one cycle spans across the screen and multiply by the time each division stands for.
symbols: the period, the time for one cycle (s or ms)
the number of divisions one cycle spans across the screen

bench.task: On a 12 V DC bench supply and a 12 V lamp (or a 1 kΩ resistor), measure voltage, current and resistance, each the right way. 12 V DC only.
check: Volts: meter across the lamp, on V DC
Amps: break the circuit, move the red lead to the A or mA socket, meter in series
Move the red lead back to V before you measure volts again
Ohms: supply off and disconnected, meter across the lamp alone
Check: volts ÷ amps should be close to the hot lamp's resistance (a cold lamp reads much lower)

bench.task: Practise prove-test-prove with your voltage indicator on a dead, isolated circuit and its proving unit (or a known live socket you are allowed to use). Do it on a circuit you have isolated and locked off yourself.
check: Check the indicator and its leads for damage
Prove it works on the proving unit or known live source
Test the isolated circuit: L–N, L–E, N–E (three-phase: every pair and each to earth)
Prove it on the proving unit again
Only then treat it as dead

cards.q: A meter is set to its 10 A range, red lead in the A socket. Someone puts the probes across a 24 V DC supply to 'check the volts'. What happens?
options: A large current flows: the meter's fuse blows
It reads 24 V, just on the wrong scale
It reads 0 A, because nothing is in series
Nothing: a meter cannot be harmed by 24 V
cards.why: On an amps range the meter is almost a short circuit, so across a supply it lets through as much current as the supply can give. On 24 V the fuse (or the supply's limit) saves it; on a distribution board the same mistake can cause an arc flash. Volts are measured across; amps in series.

cards.title: Across, in series, or dead
cards.body:
- **Volts**: across the part, in parallel. The meter has a very high resistance, so it barely disturbs the circuit.
- **Amps**: **in series**. Break the circuit and put the meter in the gap, red lead in the **A** or **mA** socket. On amps the meter has almost no resistance.
- **Ohms**: only with the circuit **dead** and preferably disconnected. The meter uses its own battery; outside voltage spoils the reading or damages it.

After measuring amps, move the red lead back to V straight away.
cards.more:
Think of a water main. To read the pressure (volts) you fit a gauge to a tapping on the side: no water flows through it. To read the flow (amps), all the water has to go through the flow meter, so you cut the pipe and put it in line.

The flow meter has a wide-open bore so it does not restrict the flow. Fit that wide-open meter across from the main to the drain instead and the main empties through it: that is a meter on amps across a supply.

Most meter accidents are a lead left in the A socket from the last job. Some meters beep a warning when the lead is in A and the dial is on V.

cards.q: How do you measure the current a 24 V DC sensor draws with a multimeter?
options: Break the circuit and put the meter in series on mA
Put the meter across the sensor on its mA range
Put the meter across the sensor on its V range
Measure its resistance and work it out live
cards.why: All the current must flow through the meter, so it goes in series, on a current range and socket. Across the sensor on mA it would short the supply.

cards.title: CAT ratings and GS38 leads
cards.body:
Where a meter is used decides how big a voltage spike it may meet. **CAT ratings** (IEC 61010) say where it is safe:

- **CAT II**: socket outlets and plug-in appliances
- **CAT III**: the fixed installation: distribution boards, panels, hard-wired motors
- **CAT IV**: the origin: the supply intake, meters, overhead lines

Choose one rated for the highest place you could use it, at or above the voltage there. The **leads** need a rating too, and **HSE GS38** asks for shrouded probes with finger guards, no more than **4 mm** of exposed tip, and fused or current-limited leads.
cards.more:
A spike from lightning or from switching a big load is much bigger near the supply intake than at a socket at the end of a long circuit, because the wiring in between soaks some of it up. A CAT IV meter is built to survive (and not explode in your hand) where the spikes are biggest.

The number after the category is the working voltage: CAT III 600 V is fine for 400 V three-phase in a panel; CAT II 1000 V is not, however big the 1000 looks, because CAT II is only tested for socket-level spikes.

GS38 tips: long bare probe tips can bridge two terminals and start an arc. 4 mm or less, and finger guards so your hand cannot slide onto the metal.

cards.q: You will measure 400 V three-phase inside a control panel fed from the building's distribution board. Which meter rating is the minimum?
options: CAT III 600 V
CAT II 1000 V
CAT II 600 V
CAT I 1000 V
cards.why: A panel is part of the fixed installation: CAT III. 600 V covers 400 V. CAT II 1000 V has a bigger number but is only built for socket-level spikes.

cards.title: Prove dead: prove, test, prove
cards.body:
Before touching anything you have isolated, prove it dead with an **approved two-pole voltage indicator** (GS38 recommends one over a multimeter, which can be on the wrong range):

1. **Prove** the indicator works, on a proving unit or a known live source.
2. **Test** the circuit: every conductor to every other and each to earth (L–N, L–E, N–E; on three-phase, every pair too).
3. **Prove** the indicator again.

The second prove shows it did not fail while testing. A dead reading from a broken tester is the reading that kills.
cards.more:
Why the indicator, not your multimeter? A multimeter left on ohms or amps, or with a blown fuse, or a lead in the wrong socket, can read nothing on a live circuit. A voltage indicator does one job and has no ranges to get wrong.

Why prove it twice? If you only prove it before, it could fail during the test (a lead breaks inside its insulation) and show 'dead' on a live circuit. Proving it afterwards closes that gap: if it still works on the proving unit, it was working when it said dead.

And test every combination, including to earth: a fault can make the neutral or the earth live, and a three-phase circuit can have one phase still fed.

cards.q: Put proving dead in order.
items: Isolate the circuit and lock it off
Prove the voltage indicator on a proving unit
Test every conductor to every other and to earth
Prove the voltage indicator on the proving unit again
cards.why: Isolate first, then prove-test-prove. The second prove is what makes the 'dead' reading trustworthy.

cards.title: Clamp meters
cards.body:
A **clamp meter** reads current without breaking the circuit: its jaws sense the **magnetic field** round a conductor.

Clamp **one** conductor. Round a whole cable (L and N together, or all three phases), the currents going out and coming back cancel, and it reads nearly **zero**: only what is leaking to earth. That is how an **earth-leakage** clamp works, on purpose.

For drive outputs and switch-mode supplies, use a **true RMS** meter: the current is not a clean sine wave, and an average-responding meter can read well out.
cards.more:
Every current makes a magnetic field round its wire. Clamp one wire and the jaws gather that field: more current, more field, bigger reading.

Now clamp both wires of a lamp circuit. 2 A goes out along L and 2 A comes back along N. Their fields point opposite ways and cancel: 0 A. If 30 mA is leaking to earth, only 1.97 A comes back on N, and the clamp shows the 30 mA difference.

Average-responding meters measure the average and multiply by a factor that is only right for a sine wave. A drive's input current comes in sharp peaks, and such a meter can read 30% or more low. A **true RMS** meter measures the heating effect, whatever the shape.

cards.q: A clamp round a whole 3-core motor cable reads about 0 A with the motor running. Why?
options: The three phase currents add to almost nothing
The motor is not drawing any current at all
Clamp meters can only read DC currents
The cable's insulation blocks the field
cards.why: The clamp reads the net current through its jaws. In a balanced three-phase load the three currents add to zero at every instant, so their fields cancel. Clamp one core at a time.

cards.title: Reading an oscilloscope
cards.body:
An **oscilloscope** draws a voltage against time. The screen is a grid of **divisions**.

- **Up**: volts per division (V/div). Peak-to-peak = divisions from trough to crest × V/div.
- **Across**: time per division (s/div, ms/div, µs/div). The **period** $T$ = divisions for one cycle × time/div.
- **Frequency**: $f = \frac{1}{T}$, with $T$ in seconds.

The **trigger** holds the picture still by starting each sweep at the same point on the wave.
cards.more:
It is a graph drawn fast, over and over. Each square across is a slice of time, each square up a slice of voltage.

Say a wave repeats every 4 squares across, at 5 ms per square: one cycle takes 20 ms. In one second (1000 ms) that fits $1000 \div 20 = 50$ times: 50 Hz. Or $\frac{1}{0.020} = 50$.

If it goes from 3 squares below the middle to 3 above, that is 6 squares at, say, 100 V per square: 600 V peak to peak, 300 V peak.

Without the trigger, each sweep starts at a random point and the wave smears across the screen.

cards.q: The scope is at {t} ms/div. One cycle of the wave spans {d} divisions. What is its frequency?
cards.why: Period = divisions × time per division. Frequency = 1 ÷ period, with the period in seconds: 1000 ÷ the period in ms.
cards.hint: Find the period first, then f = 1 ÷ T (in seconds).

cards.title: The scope's earth clip is earthed
cards.body:
On a mains-powered scope, the **earth clip** of every probe is joined to the **mains earth** through the scope's plug.

Clip it onto a point that is not at earth (a live conductor, the DC bus of a drive, the output of a supply that is not earth-referenced) and you have made a **short circuit to earth** through the probe lead: a flash, burnt leads, a damaged scope.

For such points use a **differential probe**, or a scope with **isolated** channels. Never lift the scope's earth to 'make it work'.
cards.more:
The probe tip measures; the earth clip is the reference, and on a bench scope that reference is the building's earth, solid.

On a circuit whose 0 V is earthed, clipping to 0 V is clipping earth to earth: no harm. On a drive's DC bus, the − rail sits hundreds of volts away from earth. Clip there and the bus discharges through the clip lead into the scope's earth: the lead vaporises.

A differential probe measures between its two inputs, neither of which is earthed, and hands the scope a safe, earth-referenced copy. Removing the scope's earth (a 'cheater' plug) instead makes the whole metal case live: never do it.

cards.q: You want to see the voltage across the DC bus of a drive with a bench oscilloscope. What do you use?
options: A differential probe
A standard ×10 probe, earth clip on DC−
A standard ×1 probe, earth clip on DC+
A ×10 probe, after lifting the scope's earth
cards.why: Neither DC rail is at earth, so a standard probe's earth clip on either is a short circuit to earth. A differential probe (or an isolated scope) measures between two points safely. Lifting the earth makes the scope's case live.

cards.q: A scope at 2 V/div and 0.5 ms/div shows a square wave: 5 divisions from bottom to top, and one cycle every 4 divisions. What are its peak-to-peak voltage and its frequency?
cards.why: Up times volts per division; across times time per division; then one over the period, in seconds.

cards.q: Why does step 3 turn the 2 ms into 0.002 s before working out the frequency?
cards.model: Hertz means cycles per second, so the period has to be in seconds for 1 ÷ T to come out in hertz. 1 ÷ 2 would be 0.5, and that is cycles per millisecond, not per second. 0.5 per millisecond is 500 per second, the same answer, but only if you remember to scale it.
points: So T must be in seconds

cards.q: A scope at 5 V/div and 10 µs/div shows a sine wave 3.4 divisions from trough to crest, with one cycle every 5 divisions. What are its peak and its frequency?

steps.ask: The peak (half of peak to peak, for a wave centred on zero).

cards.why: µs is $10^{-6}$ s: forgetting it gives an answer a million times out.

cards.q: A scope set to {v} V/div shows a wave {d} divisions from trough to crest. What is the peak-to-peak voltage?
cards.why: Divisions up times volts per division. (With a ×10 probe, check the scope knows: most do, if you tell it.)

cards.q: Why must a resistance reading be taken with the circuit dead?
options: The meter drives its own small current; outside voltage spoils it
Resistance only exists when no current is flowing
The meter reads in kilohms only when it is dead
So that the reading includes the supply's resistance
cards.why: On ohms the meter passes a tiny known current from its battery and measures the voltage it makes. Any other voltage in the circuit adds to that and gives a wrong reading, and can damage the meter.

cards.q: An electrician describes how they proved a panel dead. One step is wrong. Which?
lines: Isolated the panel at the main switch and fitted my lock
Proved my voltage indicator on the proving unit
Tested L1–L2, L2–L3, L1–L3, each phase to N and each to earth: all dead
cards.fix: Proved the voltage indicator on the proving unit again, then started work
cards.why: The second prove is missing. Without it, a tester that failed during the test would show 'dead' on a live panel, and nothing would catch it.

cards.q: Which CAT rating applies to measuring at the incoming supply cut-out and meter of a building?
options: CAT IV
CAT III
CAT II
CAT I
cards.why: The origin of the installation (intake, meter, cut-out) sees the biggest spikes: CAT IV. Distribution boards and panels beyond it are CAT III; sockets and plug-in appliances CAT II.

cards.q: A single-phase heater draws {i} A on its line conductor. A clamp round L and N together reads {ma} mA. How much current is coming back on the neutral?
cards.why: Round both, the clamp reads the difference between out and back: the current leaking to earth. What comes back on N is the line current less that leakage.
cards.hint: The clamp shows out minus back.

cards.q: Two clamp meters on the same drive's input cable read 8.2 A and 11.1 A. One is true RMS. Which is more likely right, and why?
options: 11.1 A: true RMS handles the peaky current
8.2 A: true RMS meters always read lower
8.2 A: average meters ignore the harmonics
Neither: clamps cannot read drive currents
cards.why: A drive's input current comes in sharp peaks. An average-responding meter assumes a sine wave and reads it low; a true RMS meter measures its real heating value. So the higher reading here is the true RMS one.

cards.q: A PWM signal repeats every {d} divisions at {t} µs/div. What is its frequency, in kHz?
cards.why: 1 ÷ (period in µs) is in MHz, so × 1000 for kHz: 1000 ÷ the period in µs.
cards.hint: Period in µs, then 1000 ÷ period gives kHz.

cards.q: Match each job with the instrument for it.
pairs: Current in one core, without breaking it
The shape of a PWM signal
A coil's resistance, off the circuit
cards.why: Each tool does one job best. A multimeter can do several, which is exactly why it is not the tool to trust for proving dead.

cards.q: Mains at {f} Hz. How many milliseconds is one cycle?
cards.why: The same rule run backwards: period = 1 ÷ frequency. Handy for setting a scope: 20 ms a cycle at 50 Hz, so 5 ms/div shows one cycle in 4 divisions.

cards.q: A meter in series with a lamp reads 0.5 A. You switch it to volts without moving the red lead from the A socket, and put it across the lamp. What does it do?
options: Shorts the lamp out through the amps socket
Reads the lamp's voltage normally
Reads 0 V, because the dial is on volts
Reads the current again, in volts
cards.why: The red lead in the A socket connects the probes through the low-resistance current shunt, whatever the dial says on many meters. Across the lamp it shorts it out. Always move the lead back to V.

cards.q: Why must a meter on its amps range never go across a supply?
options: On amps it is nearly a short circuit
On amps it can only read currents below 1 A
On amps it reverses the supply's polarity
On amps it reads the supply's voltage wrongly
cards.why: The amps range is a very low resistance so it does not disturb the current it measures in series. Across a supply, it lets through all the current the supply can give.

cards.q: One cycle spans {d} divisions at {t} ms/div. What is the frequency?
cards.why: Period = divisions × time/div; frequency = 1 ÷ period in seconds.

cards.q: Put proving dead in order.
items: Prove the indicator on a known source
Test between every conductor and to earth
Prove the indicator on the known source again
cards.why: Prove, test, prove.

cards.q: Match each place with the lowest CAT rating for a meter used there.
pairs: A plug-in appliance at a socket
